title: Hopkinsville
summary: Hopkinsville began when Bartholomew Wood, who claimed a Christian County tract in 1796, and his wife Martha Ann gave land and a share of Old Rock Spring.
bodyMarkdown:
Hopkinsville is the county seat of Christian County in southwestern Kentucky. Bartholomew Wood claimed the land where [Hopkinsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopkinsville,_Kentucky) now stands in 1796 as part of a 1,200-acre grant for his service in the American Revolution. He and his wife, Martha Ann, came from Jonesborough, Tennessee, and lived in three different homes as the settlement grew.

## A county seat at Rock Spring

[Christian County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hopkinsville,_Kentucky) was formed from Logan County on December 13, 1796. In 1797 the Woods gave 5 acres of land and a half interest in their Old Rock Spring for the county seat. By 1798 a log courthouse, a jail and a "stray pen" for loose livestock had been built.

In 1799 John Campbell and Samuel Means laid out the streets of the place, then called "Christian Court House." Residents tried to rename it "Elizabeth" after the Woods' eldest daughter. But [Elizabethtown](/stories/elizabethtown-from-severns-valley/) already had that name, so the plan failed.

## Named for Samuel Hopkins

In 1804 the Kentucky General Assembly established the town as Hopkinsville. It was named for Samuel Hopkins, a Revolutionary War veteran from Henderson County. Hopkins County is also named for him, although Hopkinsville was never its county seat.

[Samuel Hopkins](https://history.ky.gov/markers/gen-samuel-hopkins) was born in Virginia in 1753 and served on George Washington's staff. He came to Kentucky in 1797 as an agent of the Transylvania Company and helped lay out the town of [Henderson](/stories/henderson-at-red-banks/). He was [badly wounded](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/388) at the Battle of Germantown and was taken prisoner at Charleston. He served in both houses of the Kentucky legislature and in Congress, and he died in 1819.

## Hard chapters

The [Trail of Tears](/stories/mantle-rock-and-the-trail-of-tears/) passed through Hopkinsville in 1838 during the forced removal of the Cherokee. The Cherokee leaders Whitepath and Fly Smith died on that journey. Their graves are marked in the town's Trail of Tears Commemorative Park.

During the Civil War, control of the town changed hands at least half a dozen times. In December 1864, Confederate troops under Gen. Hylan B. Lyon burned the Christian County courthouse, which the Union army was using as a barracks.

Hopkinsville sat in the dark-tobacco region known as the Black Patch. On December 7, 1907, during a fight over tobacco prices, about 250 masked Night Riders seized the town's police station and burned three warehouses.

## Kentucky today

Hopkinsville is still Christian County's seat, and in 2020 it had 31,180 people. The Trail of Tears Commemorative Park preserves part of the route and honors the Cherokee who passed through.
